headline: Secret Board Talks, Big Payday: Inside GM’s CEO Succession Plans
author: David Welch

paragraphs.text: (Bloomberg) -- General Motors Co.'s strategy was clear: bring on a tech executive with software and self-driving smarts, and give them a shot at earning the automaker's top job.

It's a plan that has put Sterling Anderson in a strong position to succeed Mary Barra, GM's chief executive officer since 2014, when the moment is right. People familiar with the board's thinking say the prevailing idea is GM's next leader should be savvy in the very areas that Anderson concentrates on as global product chief.

The question is whether Anderson, who's 43 and been with GM for just shy of 18 months, is ready to step up and lead its tens of thousands of engineers and union workers into a highly uncertain future for the global auto industry. Barra and GM's board have been mulling the timing of naming a new CEO and transitioning to new leadership, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the discussions are private. The courses of action could include Barra staying on beyond this year as CEO or becoming GM's executive chair.

People familiar with the matter say Anderson recently did a round of one-on-one meetings with board directors, though the exact purpose is unclear. The company also has been working for more than a month with the executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help evaluate potential external candidates, the people said.
A GM spokesperson declined to comment.

Anderson has been busy since GM poached him from Aurora Innovation Inc., the startup he co-founded with the former head of Google's self-driving car project. He's led an initiative to cut GM's vehicle development cycle in half. He rehired key personnel from Cruise, the robotaxi operation GM shuttered months before he joined the company, and revived efforts to build autonomous vehicles. By 2028, the goal is to deliver a Cadillac that can safely coast on its own without a driver's hands on the wheel or eyes on the road.

GM's board, chaired by Barra since 2016, is weighing that early record against a range of factors. For one, there's no rush to usher Barra out of the CEO seat she's occupied since January 2014. While the company's normal retirement age is 65, and Barra will celebrate that birthday on Christmas Eve, there's no mandate for her to bow out.

The board also has internal alternatives. Chief Financial Officer Paul Jacobson is interested in the top job and could be considered if the board opts to give Anderson more time to settle in, people familiar with the matter said. While the 54-year-old former Delta Air Lines Inc. CFO is well liked by Wall Street, financial proficiency is a lesser priority. Barra and GM's directors are more interested in finding leadership with command of the role software is playing in controlling modern vehicles, as well as how advances in artificial intelligence will define transportation for years to come, the people said.
President Mark Reuss, a 63-year-old GM lifer, may also play a major role in a transition, but at his age is less likely to be CEO.

"I'm not convinced she is going to leave, nor do I think she should," Jeffrey Sonnenfeld, a Yale School of Management professor, said of Barra. The two speak roughly half a dozen times a year. "She has done very well and we have other successful companies being led by leaders past 65."

This is a critical juncture for GM to be working out who will lead the carmaker into a next era. Chinese manufacturers have been flooding virtually all major auto markets other than the US with millions of vehicles, further crowding an already congested industry that's long grappled with chronic overcapacity.

While GM has been able to count on refuge from Washington, which has put up barriers to Chinese imports, President Donald Trump has on multiple occasions indicated a willingness to let the likes of BYD Co. or Geely Automobile Holdings Ltd. in, as long as they manufacture locally. Even if China's automakers end up steering clear or are kept at bay, GM and its peers are increasingly reliant on a US new-car market that has never been more expensive and is close to peak levels of demand.

GM's answer to these challenges has been to try to match its Chinese counterparts on costs and speed to market. Anderson has played a lead role in the company's push to use AI and digital tools to reduce its vehicle development time to two years, down from four.

The automaker also is trying to get back into the automated driving game after its robotaxi unit Cruise imploded two years ago. Anderson, who as a direct report to Elon Musk led the team that delivered Tesla Inc.'s Autopilot, has invigorated GM's development of Super Cruise, a hands-free system now generating billions of dollars of subscription revenue.

While Anderson may have the technology background GM seeks, less than two years ago he was the second-in-command at Aurora, an autonomous trucking startup with only around 2,000 employees. GM has single factories with double that staff.

Auto industry succession has always been thorny, in part due to the breadth of expertise required spanning product, sales, engineering, manufacturing and more. It can also be a tough sell nowadays, because with the exception of Tesla, carmakers' market valuations pale in comparison to tech giants.

Anderson was brought in with an annual pay package set at $16 million, the majority of which is stock-based and vests over time. He also was awarded one-time cash and at-risk stock awards totaling $24 million as part of his new-hire package. This meant Anderson's compensation package exceeded $40 million last year, surpassing Barra's total, which was just shy of $30 million.

Barra has been opening up lanes for her direct reports to shine. When GM has hosted new vehicle and tech showcases in New York the past two years, the CEO has kicked off festivities, then handed off the mic to Anderson to do most of the talking. She's taken a similar approach to earnings calls, with Jacobson getting most of the airtime with Wall Street analysts.
Anderson also has planted a flag in Michigan. He moved to the Detroit area this year and no longer commutes in from Silicon Valley.

Barra is preparing to hand over the reins having racked up major achievements, most notably getting GM in the game with electrification and hands-free driving. She also navigated a faulty ignition switch crisis that erupted almost immediately after she started as CEO.
There also have been some major missteps.

The company's electric vehicle program is in a strong position if Americans start to shift to plug-ins anytime soon, but this has come at great cost. GM has shelled out some $35 billion on EVs and autonomous driving, with little in the way of early return on investment.

GM was far from alone in plowing billions into EVs that have sold in underwhelming volumes, but Barra went long by developing a dozen models and aiming to sell 1 million a year. The company's sales have come nowhere near that level, even before Trump pulled the rug out from the EV market by ending incentive programs and gutting fuel economy and emissions regulations.

The company has written down more than $11 billion of its EV investments, and after spending over $10 billion to acquire and grow Cruise, shut the operation down after one if its cars dragged a woman and regulators grounded its fleet.

GM's stock price was static for much of Barra's tenure. Over the past three years, it has more than doubled as the automaker bought back $29 billion in shares. GM has taken some political heat from progressive Democrats including Massachusetts Senator Elizabeth Warren and Michigan Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed for recently authorizing another $20 billion worth of repurchases.
Those moves largely came under the direction of Jacobson. If he pushes for the job, GM's recent share performance bolsters his case.
When asked at a Barclays investor conference this week about potential leadership transition, Jacobson reiterated comments Barra has made about still being invigorated by the job.

"As Mary has said very publicly, she's got a lot of energy for this," Jacobson said. "I can vouch for that. Some day she has more energy than I do, and that's evidenced by the grilling that I get from time to time. She's here, she's fully engaged, and I expect that to continue."
